## Using This Outline

Use these questions to plan the Written Research Proposal for
[Project 2](../../syllabus/project_2_prompt.qmd). The final submission is
**one 2-4 page paper in paragraph form**, with subheadings. This outline is
a planning aid and is not a separate submission.

**You are proposing a study. You will not carry out the research, collect data,
or perform analysis for this project.** Describe the decisions you would make
and explain your reasons. Use future or conditional language throughout.

## 1. Decision Context

Who would use the study's results? What problem, opportunity, or decision
would those results address? Explain why the decision matters.

## 2. Research Question

Write a focused question. Identify the population or setting, the topic or
outcome, and any comparison that matters. Explain how an answer would help
the decision maker.

## 3. Research Objectives

Identify what you would need to learn to answer the question. Objectives
might describe a population, compare groups, assess a relationship, or
evaluate a proposed change.

Use objectives to clarify the research question. They can be included in
that section of your paper rather than submitted separately.

## 4. Population, Concepts, and Measures

Define the population and the unit you would study, such as a person,
organization, transaction, or event.

Identify the main concepts. For each one, explain what it means in your
study and how you would measure it. For survey questions, consider the
wording, response options, and measurement scale. If you propose using
existing records, explain what one row represents and which fields you
would need.

## 5. Proposed Study Design

Choose and explain the approach you would use, such as a survey, observational
study, experiment, or predictive study.

Describe how you would select participants or records, collect information,
and organize the study. For an experiment, explain the treatment, comparison,
and assignment process. Identify practical requirements such as access,
time, or resources.

Do not recruit participants, distribute a survey, gather records, or conduct
the study. This section describes your plan.

## 6. Quality of the Evidence

Consider who the sample would represent and who might be missed. Discuss
selection, nonresponse, measurement error, and other sources of bias that
matter for your proposed study.

Explain what conclusions the design could support. Distinguish association
from causation, and identify limits on applying the findings to other people
or settings.

## 7. Proposed Analysis, If Helpful

You may briefly describe how you would summarize the proposed information
or assess a relationship. Explain why those methods would fit the question
and measures.

This detail is optional. You do not need to run a test, calculate a statistic,
build a model, or produce results.

## 8. Risks, Limitations, and Ethics

Identify specific risks and how you would address them. Consider consent,
privacy, fairness, possible harm, and exclusion.

Explain which limitations would remain and what they would mean for the
study's conclusions.

## 9. Pitch and Feedback

Prepare to explain your question and design to the other teams in your
small set. During the pitch and critique exercise, record the concerns
raised, your responses, and the changes you plan to make.

Every team will have a turn presenting and critiquing another proposal.

## 10. Revise the Written Proposal

Use the Week 13 discussion and Week 14 feedback to revise the paper.
Organize it around the required components in the
[Project 2 prompt](../../syllabus/project_2_prompt.qmd).

The [rubric](../../syllabus/project_2_rubric.qmd) scores four aspects of the
same written proposal. You submit one complete paper, not four separate
written assignments.
